assessment_style: freeCodeCamp-style: progressive MCQ checkpoints (theory, logic, syntax) per lesson, each lesson capped by an applied coding challenge
note_on_relationship_to_existing_quiz: This assessment is a SEPARATE, additive practice layer.

theory_mcq.question: Why does a segment tree array need 4n elements rather than the seemingly sufficient 2n?
options: 4n is an arbitrary safety margin; 2n always works

2n IS sufficient when n is a PERFECT POWER OF 2 (complete binary tree has 2n-1 nodes fitting in indices 1..2n-1); but when n is NOT a power of 2, the tree is INCOMPLETE and some bottom-level nodes require higher indices than 2n-1; for n=5 (height=3), the maximum node index reaches 2^(h+1)-1 = 15 < 4*5=20; the derivation: height h=ceil(log2(n)), max index = 2^(h+1)-1 <= 4n holds for all n; 4n is the universal safe bound covering all cases without needing to compute the exact required size
4n is required because segment trees store both values and parent pointers
The extra 2n space is used by the lazy propagation array in all variants
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's derivation: 'For n not a power of 2: 2^(h+1) <= 4n (by definition of ceil(log2)); For n=5: h=3, 2^4=16 <= 4*5=20 ✓' — 4n is the universal safe bound; for n=9: h=4, 2^5=32 <= 4*9=36 ✓; the extra space is wasted for power-of-2 n but prevents buffer overflows for all other n.

theory_mcq.question: The segment tree build is O(n) because 'each of the 2n-1 nodes is computed exactly once'. Why are there exactly 2n-1 nodes?
options: A balanced binary tree always has exactly n nodes

A FULL BINARY TREE with n LEAF NODES has exactly n-1 INTERNAL NODES (a well-known tree property: in any full binary tree — where every non-leaf has exactly 2 children — internal nodes = leaves - 1); total nodes = n leaves + (n-1) internal = 2n-1; the segment tree is a full binary tree by construction (each non-leaf always has exactly 2 children representing left and right halves); thus 2n-1 nodes are computed during build = O(n) work
The build recurses n times, each taking O(1), giving O(n)
2n-1 nodes come from the 4n array having half its entries unused
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'O(n) build: each of the 2n-1 nodes computed exactly once' — the full binary tree property (internal = leaves - 1) gives total = 2n-1; each node computation is O(1) (combine two children); total build work = O(2n-1) = O(n); this is why segment tree build is linear despite the tree having O(n) height.

logic_mcq.question: For segment tree on [1,3,5,7,9,11] (n=6), what is stored at node 1 (root) and why?
options: Root stores 36 (sum of all elements: 1+3+5+7+9+11=36) — confirmed
Root stores 1 (the first element)
Root stores 6 (the count of elements)
Root stores 11 (the maximum element)
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: tree[1]=36 for sum segment tree on [1,3,5,7,9,11]; the root covers the entire range [0,5] and stores the aggregate (sum) of all elements; 1+3+5+7+9+11=36; this is the defining property of the root node — it covers the full array range.

logic_mcq.question: In the build recursion, `this.tree[node] = this.tree[2*node] + this.tree[2*node+1]` runs AFTER the two child calls. Why must it come after (not before)?
options: The order is arbitrary; the tree values are the same either way

BOTTOM-UP computation: a node's aggregate depends on its CHILDREN'S aggregates, which in turn depend on THEIR children's aggregates; combining before recursing would use uninitialized values (still 0 from fill(0)); the correct order is: recursively build left subtree → recursively build right subtree → combine results; this is POST-ORDER traversal where the parent's computation happens AFTER both subtrees are fully populated
Combining before recursion would create infinite loops
JavaScript requires sequential array access; out-of-order access causes memory errors
logic_mcq.explanation: Post-order construction is fundamental: the combine step `tree[node] = tree[2*node] + tree[2*node+1]` reads tree[2*node] and tree[2*node+1] which are only correct after their respective subtrees are built; doing this before the recursive calls would combine zeros (initial fill values), not the actual subtree aggregates.

syntax_mcq.question: The tree is 1-indexed (root at index 1) rather than 0-indexed. What is the KEY ADVANTAGE of 1-indexing for tree navigation?
options: 1-indexing prevents off-by-one errors in the mid computation

1-INDEXING enables PURE ARITHMETIC NAVIGATION without conditional checks: left child = 2*node, right child = 2*node+1, parent = Math.floor(node/2); these formulas work perfectly for all valid indices; if the root were at 0: left child = 2*0+1=1, right = 2*0+2=2 — navigation still works but the formulas become 2*node+1 and 2*node+2 (less elegant); 1-indexing makes the Fenwick tree even more natural (operations rely on bit manipulations of 1-indexed positions); 0-indexed would leave index 0 permanently wasted anyway
1-indexing allows using 0 as a sentinel value in the tree array
1-indexing enables O(1) parent lookup without storing parent pointers
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Array representation: root at index 1, left child = 2*i, right child = 2*i+1' — the 2*i and 2*i+1 formulas work cleanly only when the root is at index 1; with root at 0, formulas become 2*i+1 and 2*i+2 (still correct but less intuitive); the 1-indexed convention is universal for array-represented binary trees.

theory_mcq.question: Why does a range query visit at most O(log n) nodes despite potentially spanning many elements?
options: The query prunes entire subtrees when they are fully inside or fully outside the query range

QUERY DECOMPOSITION: at each level of the tree, the query range [ql,qr] can produce at most 2 PARTIAL OVERLAPS (one on the left boundary, one on the right boundary); every other node at that level is either FULLY INSIDE (return stored value immediately) or FULLY OUTSIDE (return identity immediately); with O(log n) levels and at most 2 active nodes per level: at most 2*log(n) nodes are visited total; this O(log n) bound is tight — a query range that spans exactly half the array visits exactly O(log n) nodes
The query uses binary search to find the boundaries, reducing to O(log n)
Range queries are O(log n) because the tree has height log n
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Query decomposition: split [ql,qr] into at most 2*log(n) stored ranges' — the key insight is that per level, at most 2 nodes straddle the query boundary (partial overlap → recurse); all other nodes in the query range are completely inside and returned in O(1); height=log n → at most 2*log(n) nodes visited total.

theory_mcq.question: In `update(idx, val)`, why must `this.tree[node] = this.tree[2*node] + this.tree[2*node+1]` be called on the WAY BACK UP?
options: The combine step on the way back is optional if the leaf was correctly set

BOTTOM-UP PROPAGATION: when a leaf value changes, all ANCESTORS of that leaf have incorrect aggregates; the update descends to the leaf (setting it correctly), then as the recursion returns (back up the path), each ancestor is RECOMPUTED using its two children's current values; all other nodes in the tree are unaffected because only the ancestors of the changed leaf have that leaf in their range; O(log n) recompute steps on the way back = O(log n) total update cost
The combine runs bottom-up to propagate the lazy tag
Without recomputing, the tree structure becomes invalid and future queries fail
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's trace: 'BACK: tree[4]=tree[8]+tree[9]=1+10=11; BACK: tree[2]=tree[4]+tree[5]=11+5=16; BACK: tree[1]=tree[2]+tree[3]=16+27=43' — each ancestor on the leaf-to-root path is recomputed using the now-correct children; only log(n) ancestors exist, giving O(log n) total update.

logic_mcq.question: For `query(0, 2)` on [1,3,5,7,9,11], the result is 9. Which NODES does the query visit and what does it return from each?
options: node1[0,5]: partial; node2[0,2]: fully inside → return 9; total = 9 ✓
node1[0,5]: fully inside → return 36
Visits all 11 nodes; sums leaf values 1+3+5=9
node1[0,5]: partial; node2[0,2]: partial; node4[0,1]: inside→4; node5[2,2]: inside→5; returns 4+5=9
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: query(0,2)=9; at node1 [0,5]: ql=0,qr=2 partially overlaps → recurse; at node2 [0,2]: ql=0<=l=0 AND r=2<=qr=2 → FULLY INSIDE → return tree[2]=9 immediately; at node3 [3,5]: qr=2<l=3 → FULLY OUTSIDE → return 0; total=9+0=9; the query only visits nodes 1, 2, and 3 (3 nodes for a 6-element tree).

logic_mcq.question: After `update(1, 10)` on [1,3,5,7,9,11], the trace shows nodes [9,4,2,1] are updated. Verify `query(1,4)` returns 31.
options: query(1,4)=3+5+7+9=24 (stale pre-update value)
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: query(1,4)=31 after update(1,10); updated array=[1,10,5,7,9,11]; sum of indices 1..4 = 10+5+7+9=31; the update correctly propagated through nodes 9→4→2→1 (leaf to root path for index 1).

syntax_mcq.question: The query uses `if (qr < l || r < ql) return 0` as the FULLY OUTSIDE base case. Why return 0 specifically (not -1 or null)?
options: 0 is returned because null or undefined would cause arithmetic errors

0 is the ADDITIVE IDENTITY for SUM queries: adding 0 to any partial result leaves it unchanged; returning 0 for an out-of-range subtree correctly contributes nothing to the total sum; for MINIMUM queries, the identity would be +Infinity (min(any, Infinity) = any); for MAXIMUM queries, -Infinity; the identity element MUST match the aggregate function — using 0 for min would incorrectly make empty ranges contribute 0 to min computations; the correct identity ensures the partial-overlap recursion correctly combines results
0 is returned because the tree is initialised with 0 (fill(0))
0 signals to the parent that no contribution was made from this subtree
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Identity values: 0 for sum, Infinity for min, -Infinity for max' — the out-of-range return value must be the identity element for the aggregate function; for sum: 0+x=x (correct); for min: min(Infinity,x)=x (correct); using the wrong identity corrupts results — e.g., returning 0 for min queries would make any query that hits an out-of-range subtree return 0 incorrectly.

Both update and query pass node, l, r as parameters tracking the current node's range — the caller doesn't need to track this.

theory_mcq.question: Why is LAZY PROPAGATION needed for range updates, and what problem does naive range update have?
options: Lazy propagation reduces space usage by not storing all intermediate values

NAIVE RANGE UPDATE decomposes into O(n) INDIVIDUAL POINT UPDATES: updating all elements in [l,r] one by one costs O(n log n) per range update; for m range updates, total cost is O(mn log n) — too slow; LAZY PROPAGATION defers the update to child nodes until they are actually accessed: when the current node's range is FULLY INSIDE the update range, mark the node with a LAZY TAG (pending addition) and update the stored aggregate immediately without touching children; children are only updated when a query or further update REQUIRES accessing them (pushed down then)
Naive range update is incorrect; only lazy propagation gives correct results
Lazy propagation is needed only for non-commutative aggregates
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Range update problem: update all elements in [l,r] by adding delta. Naive: O(n) range update (update each element individually)' — lazy propagation achieves O(log n) range update by tagging entire subtrees with pending updates instead of propagating to every leaf; correctness is maintained by pushing down tags before any child access.

theory_mcq.question: In `pushDown(node, l, r)`, why is the SEGMENT SIZE (mid-l+1 and r-mid) multiplied by the lazy tag when updating children's tree values?
options: The size multiplication is an error; lazy tags should be added without multiplying

The lazy tag represents a PER-ELEMENT ADDITION DELTA: if lazy[node]=d, it means every element in node's range should be increased by d; the stored tree[node] is the SUM of all elements in the range; when pushing to a child covering 'len' elements: the child's sum increases by d * len (d added to each of len elements); the child's own lazy tag is incremented by d (to be further propagated when needed); without the multiplication, the sum would be wrong (only d added, not d*len)
The size multiplication handles the case where some elements were already updated
Multiplying by size converts from per-element delta to per-range delta
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `this.tree[2*node] += this.lazy[node] * leftLen` — if lazy[node]=10 and leftLen=3, the left child's sum increases by 30 (10 added to each of 3 elements); the child's lazy tag gets +=10 (propagated per-element for future pushdowns); this correctly decomposes: sum_update = delta * count, tag_update = delta (per-element).

logic_mcq.question: After `rangeUpdate(1, 3, 10)` on [1,2,3,4,5], the array becomes [1,12,13,14,5]. Verify `rangeQuery(0,4)=45` and `rangeQuery(1,3)=39`.
options: 1+12+13+14+5=45 ✓; 12+13+14=39 ✓ — confirmed by direct execution
rangeQuery(0,4)=15+30=45 but rangeQuery(1,3)=30 (only the delta)
rangeQuery(0,4)=40 (misses element 5 which wasn't updated)
rangeQuery(1,3)=36 (3 elements * 10 + original 3+4+5=12)
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: rangeQuery(0,4)=45 and rangeQuery(1,3)=39; array after update: [1,2+10,3+10,4+10,5]=[1,12,13,14,5]; total=1+12+13+14+5=45; partial [1..3]=12+13+14=39.

logic_mcq.question: Why is `pushDown` called BEFORE recursing into children in both `rangeUpdate` and `rangeQuery`?
options: pushDown is called after recursion to avoid double counting

CORRECTNESS GUARANTEE: before recursing into a child, any PENDING LAZY TAG on the current node must be propagated to the children; without pushDown first, the children's tree values would be stale (missing the pending update); a query to a child would return an incorrect value, and a further update to a child would be combined with an unaccounted-for parent delta; pushDown before recursion ensures children have CORRECT CURRENT values before any reads or writes; the invariant: if lazy[node]!=0, children's values are wrong by exactly lazy[node]*their_count
pushDown is only needed before rangeQuery, not rangeUpdate
pushDown is called before recursion to reset the lazy array
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `this.pushDown(node, l, r); // propagate before going deeper` in both methods — the lazy invariant: lazy[node] represents a pending per-element delta NOT YET reflected in children; before accessing children, this delta must be pushed; if pushDown were omitted, querying a range that partially overlaps a tagged node would read stale child values.

syntax_mcq.question: When the `rangeUpdate` range FULLY COVERS the current node's range, we do `this.tree[node] += delta * (r-l+1); this.lazy[node] += delta; return`. Why NOT recurse into children here?
options: We must always recurse into children to maintain the tree invariant

The LAZY INSIGHT: when the update range FULLY COVERS [l,r], we can update the node's SUM in O(1) without touching children; delta*len gives the exact sum change; we STORE the per-element delta in lazy[node] for LATER propagation; recursing into children now would be O(n) work (visiting all leaves); by deferring propagation, the range update costs O(log n) total; the children WILL get correct values when pushDown is called before they are next accessed; this deferral is what makes lazy propagation O(log n)
Not recursing saves memory by avoiding stack overflow
Children are not recursed into because they have correct values already
syntax_mcq.explanation: The lazy propagation insight: for a fully-covered node, the sum update is exact and immediate (tree[node] += delta*(r-l+1)), but the per-element update to children is DEFERRED via lazy[node] += delta; deferring avoids the O(n) cost of propagating to all leaves immediately; the correctness guarantee is that pushDown happens before any child access.

theory_mcq.question: LeetCode #307 offers three approaches: prefix sum, segment tree, and Fenwick tree. When should you choose SEGMENT TREE over FENWICK TREE?
options: Segment tree is always better; Fenwick tree is an inferior alternative

CHOOSE SEGMENT TREE when: (1) the aggregate is NOT a PREFIX SUM (e.g., range minimum, range maximum, range GCD, range XOR) — Fenwick trees natively support only prefix sums; (2) range updates (lazy propagation) are needed — Fenwick trees can support range updates but with more complex logic; CHOOSE FENWICK when: only prefix sums needed and the query range is always [0..r] or computed via subtraction; Fenwick uses less code (~10 lines) and less space (n vs 4n) for the prefix sum case
Segment tree should be used when n is large (>10^5)
Fenwick tree should be used for minimum queries; segment tree for maximum
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Fenwick tree alternative: simpler code, same O(log n) complexity. Practical tradeoff: Fenwick is preferred when only prefix sum is needed' — the segment tree's generality (any associative aggregate, range updates) comes at the cost of more code and 4n space; Fenwick's simplicity and efficiency for prefix sums make it the preferred choice when those constraints fit.

theory_mcq.question: The `(l+r)>>1` operation for computing mid in NumArray. Why use bit-shift instead of `Math.floor((l+r)/2)`?
options: Bit-shift is required because JavaScript doesn't have integer division

For POSITIVE INTEGERS, `(l+r)>>1` is EQUIVALENT to `Math.floor((l+r)/2)` but FASTER: the right bit-shift by 1 divides by 2 and truncates to integer in a single CPU instruction; Math.floor involves floating-point conversion, floor computation, and conversion back to integer — multiple operations; in segment tree implementations with millions of recursive calls, this constant-factor improvement matters; the two forms are identical for non-negative l and r (all valid index ranges); `>>1` is the idiomatic form in competitive programming
>>1 handles negative indices that Math.floor would compute incorrectly
>>1 prevents integer overflow when l+r exceeds 32 bits
theory_mcq.explanation: For non-negative integer indices (all valid segment tree positions), `(l+r)>>1` is exactly equivalent to `Math.floor((l+r)/2)` and is a micro-optimisation; JavaScript engines may optimise both identically in practice; the >>1 form is conventional in performance-sensitive code and explicitly signals 'integer division by 2'.

logic_mcq.question: For NumArray([1,3,5]) with `sumRange(0,2)=9` and then `update(1,2); sumRange(0,2)=8`. Verify these results.
options: Initial sum: 1+3+5=9 ✓; after update(1,2): array=[1,2,5]; 1+2+5=8 ✓
update(1,2) adds 2 to index 1: array=[1,5,5]; sum=11
sumRange(0,2) after update=9 (update not reflected yet)
sumRange(0,2)=7 after update(1,2) because index 1 changes from 3 to 2 (difference=-1)
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: sumRange(0,2)=9 (1+3+5); after update(1,2) sets index 1 to value 2: array=[1,2,5]; sumRange(0,2)=1+2+5=8; note: update(index, val) SETS the value (not adds to it); point update replaces the element.

logic_mcq.question: The complexity table shows: prefix sum has O(1) query but O(n) update. WHY is prefix sum update O(n)?
options: Prefix sum array has n entries, each taking O(1) to compute — so O(n) total

When a SINGLE ELEMENT changes, ALL PREFIX SUMS starting from that position change: if nums[i] changes by delta, then prefix[i], prefix[i+1], ..., prefix[n-1] all change by delta (since prefix[j] = sum(nums[0..j])); updating all n-i affected prefix sums requires O(n) time; this is the fundamental tradeoff — storing prefix sums enables O(1) range queries but makes updates O(n); segment trees and Fenwick trees break this tradeoff by accepting O(log n) for both
Prefix sum update rebuilds the entire array from scratch
Only the prefix sums at even indices need updating, giving O(n/2)≈O(n)
logic_mcq.explanation: The O(n) update cost of prefix sums follows from their definition: prefix[j] = sum(nums[0..j]) includes nums[i] for all j >= i; changing nums[i] invalidates all prefix[j] for j in [i, n-1] — that's n-i entries requiring recomputation; in the worst case (i=0), all n prefix sums need updating.

syntax_mcq.question: In `NumArray`, the build method is named `_build` (with underscore). What JavaScript convention does this signal?
options: _build is a JavaScript reserved keyword that forces private method syntax

UNDERSCORE PREFIX is a CONVENTIONAL SIGNAL that the method is PRIVATE or INTERNAL — not part of the public interface; JavaScript doesn't enforce true private methods by default (unlike Python or Java); `_build` tells users of the NumArray class that this method is an implementation detail, not meant to be called from outside; modern JavaScript uses `#build` (with hash) for true private fields/methods; the underscore convention predates the `#` syntax and remains common in codebases for compatibility
_build is called differently than build due to the leading underscore
Methods starting with _ are automatically memoised by JavaScript engines
syntax_mcq.explanation: The underscore prefix is a longstanding JavaScript convention (inherited from Python) signalling 'this is an internal implementation method'; it's not enforced by the language but communicates developer intent; modern JavaScript uses `#name` for actual private class fields/methods; in the NumArray context, `_build` is called only from the constructor and should not be called by external code.

theory_mcq.question: What does `lowbit(i) = i & (-i)` compute and why does it work?
options: lowbit computes the highest set bit of i

lowbit(i) isolates the LOWEST SET BIT of i: -i in two's complement is ~i+1 (invert all bits then add 1); this sets all bits BELOW the lowest set bit of i to 1 and all bits AT AND ABOVE it to 0 (except the lowest set bit itself which stays 1); i & (-i) then extracts only the lowest set bit position; example: i=6=0110, -i=1010 (two's complement), i&(-i)=0010=2 (bit 1) ✓; i=8=1000, -i=1000, i&(-i)=1000=8 (bit 3) ✓
lowbit computes floor(log2(i))
lowbit is equivalent to i modulo 2
theory_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: lowbit(6)=2, lowbit(8)=8; the two's complement explanation: -i = ~i + 1 flips all bits above the lowest set bit and sets that bit to 1 (via carry); i & (-i) then zeros everything except the shared lowest set bit; this operation is the foundation of both Fenwick update (add lowbit to move up) and query (subtract lowbit to move to prefix parent).

theory_mcq.question: In Fenwick update, `i += this.lowbit(i)` moves to the NEXT node that bit[i] CONTRIBUTES TO. In query, `i -= this.lowbit(i)` moves to the PREVIOUS PREFIX BUCKET. Why are these directions opposite?
options: The directions are arbitrary; both operations could use either direction

The Fenwick tree has an ASYMMETRIC structure: bit[i] stores the sum of a range ENDING AT i with length lowbit(i); QUERY traverses backward: to compute prefix[i]=sum(1..i), we need bit[i] (covers i-lowbit(i)+1 to i), then bit[i-lowbit(i)] (covers its own range), etc. — moving LEFT (subtracting lowbit) collects non-overlapping ranges; UPDATE traverses forward: when element i changes, all ANCESTORS whose range CONTAINS i must be updated — i contributes to bit[j] whenever j's range includes i, which happens for j = i, i+lowbit(i), i+lowbit(i)+lowbit(i+lowbit(i)), etc. — moving RIGHT (adding lowbit)
The opposite directions are needed to avoid infinite loops
Update uses addition to prevent index 0 from being accessed
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's trace: 'TRACE update(6): i=6→bit[6]+=delta, i=8→bit[8]+=delta; TRACE query(6): i=6→sum+=bit[6], i=4→sum+=bit[4], i=0 stop' — the divergent directions are inherent to the Fenwick tree's structure: update propagates upward (to all ancestors), query aggregates leftward (collecting disjoint prefix ranges); these are two different tree traversals on the same underlying structure.

logic_mcq.question: For FenwickTree on [1,3,5,7,9,11], `query(3)=9` (1+3+5). Trace the query path.
options: query(3): i=3(011), sum+=bit[3]; i-=lowbit(3)=1, i=2(010), sum+=bit[2]; i-=lowbit(2)=2, i=0, stop; total=9 ✓ (bit[3] covers pos3=5; bit[2] covers pos1-2: 1+3=4; 5+4=9)
query(3): directly returns bit[3] which equals 1+3+5=9
query(3): i=3, sum+=bit[3]=7, i=0 stop; but 7≠9
query(3) requires visiting all elements 1,2,3
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: query(3)=9; trace: i=3(011): sum+=bit[3]=5 (bit[3] covers only position 3 since lowbit(3)=1); i-=1, i=2(010): sum+=bit[2]=1+3=4 (bit[2] covers positions 1-2 since lowbit(2)=2); i-=2, i=0: stop; total=5+4=9 ✓.

logic_mcq.question: After `ft.update(2, 7)` on the Fenwick tree (adding 7 to position 2), `query(3)` returns 16. Verify.
options: After adding 7 to position 2: prefix sum 1..3 = 1+(3+7)+5 = 16 ✓
query(3)=9+7=16 (the 7 was added to the total, not position 2)
query(3) still returns 9 since Fenwick updates are lazy
query(3)=9+7*3=30 (delta applied to all 3 positions)
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: query(3)=16 after update(2,7); ft.update(2,7) adds 7 to position 2 (1-indexed), making the element at position 2 become 3+7=10; prefix sum 1..3 = 1+10+5=16 ✓; the update propagates through bit[2] and bit[4] (ancestors of position 2).

syntax_mcq.question: The Fenwick tree is 1-indexed but `buildFenwick(nums)` converts 0-indexed nums using `ft.update(i+1, nums[i])`. What would happen if `ft.update(i, nums[i])` were used (no +1)?
options: No difference — Fenwick trees can be either 0-indexed or 1-indexed

Using `ft.update(i, ...)` without +1: when i=0, the update is called with position 0; in the Fenwick update loop `while(i<=this.n)`, starting at i=0: i+=lowbit(0)=0 (since 0 & (-0) = 0 & 0 = 0) — the loop NEVER TERMINATES (infinite loop); the Fenwick tree REQUIRES 1-indexing because lowbit(0)=0 would cause the update loop to get stuck at i=0 forever; the 1-indexed convention is not just convention — it's a correctness requirement for the i+=lowbit(i) termination to work
0-indexed Fenwick trees work correctly; the +1 is a coding style preference
ft.update(0,...) would update position n (the last position) due to wrap-around
syntax_mcq.explanation: Critical correctness issue: lowbit(0) = 0 & (-0) = 0 & 0 = 0; the update loop `i += lowbit(i)` with i=0 gives i=0+0=0 → infinite loop; the query loop `i -= lowbit(i)` with i=0 gives i=0-0=0 → infinite loop; 1-indexing ensures all valid indices have non-zero lowbits, guaranteeing termination; this is why Fenwick trees are ALWAYS 1-indexed.

coding_challenges.title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement the Fenwick Tree from this lesson.
requirements: Implement `class FenwickTree` with update(i,delta) and query(i) (1-indexed)
Implement `buildFenwick(nums)` returning a FenwickTree from a 0-indexed array
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: update and query: O(log n) — at most log n iterations. buildFenwick: O(n log n). Space: O(n).

hints.text: update(i,delta): while(i<=n) bit[i]+=delta; i+=lowbit(i) — moves to ancestors.
query(i): while(i>0) sum+=bit[i]; i-=lowbit(i) — collects disjoint prefix ranges.
buildFenwick: call ft.update(i+1, nums[i]) for each element — MUST use i+1 (1-indexed).

theory_mcq.question: The SPARSE TABLE achieves O(1) query but requires the aggregate function to be IDEMPOTENT. What does idempotent mean and why is it required?
options: Idempotent means the function returns the same value for the same input (like identity)

IDEMPOTENT means f(x, x) = x — applying the function to the SAME VALUE twice gives the same result; min(x,x)=x and max(x,x)=x are idempotent; sum is NOT idempotent (x+x=2x≠x); sparse table achieves O(1) query by using TWO OVERLAPPING POWER-OF-2 RANGES that together cover [l,r]; since the ranges overlap, some elements are counted TWICE; for idempotent functions (min/max), counting twice is harmless; for sum, counting an element twice gives the wrong answer — which is why sparse table doesn't support sum queries with O(1) time
Idempotent means the function is commutative (order doesn't matter)
Idempotent functions are required for O(n log n) build time
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Sparse table: O(n log n) build, O(1) query for idempotent functions (min/max)' — the O(1) query trick: find k=floor(log2(r-l+1)), then min(table[l][k], table[r-(1<<k)+1][k]); the two ranges [l, l+2^k-1] and [r-2^k+1, r] overlap but min(a,min(a,b))=min(a,b) by idempotency; if sum were used: sum(a, sum(a,b)) = 2a+b ≠ a+b (wrong).

theory_mcq.question: For the decision guide: given 'range min queries, NO updates', which structure is optimal and why?
options: Segment tree — it handles all cases including static arrays

SPARSE TABLE: when there are NO UPDATES, the array is STATIC and the sparse table's O(n log n) build cost is paid once; queries are O(1) per query — faster than segment tree's O(log n); for q queries: sparse table costs O(n log n + q) vs segment tree's O(n + q log n); when q is large, sparse table wins decisively; for dynamic arrays (with updates), sparse table cannot efficiently update (O(n log n) per update makes it impractical) — segment tree or lazy segment tree is required
Fenwick tree — it handles all range queries in O(log n)
Prefix sum — it has O(1) query for all aggregate types
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's decision guide: 'if !hasUpdates && (queryType==='min'||queryType==='max') return Sparse Table O(n log n) build, O(1) query' — the No-Updates + min/max combination makes sparse table the clear winner; its O(1) per query advantage over segment tree's O(log n) is decisive for query-heavy workloads; static arrays are the prerequisite since sparse table rebuild is prohibitively expensive.

logic_mcq.question: For `sparseTableQuery(st, 2, 5)` on [3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6], the result is 1. Verify using the range [2..5]=[4,1,5,9].
options: Range [2..5] = [4,1,5,9]; min = 1 ✓; k=floor(log2(4))=2; table[2][2]=min(arr[2..5])=1; table[5-4+1=2][2] also covers position 2; result=min(1,1)=1 ✓
sparseTableQuery(2,5) returns 4 (the first element in the range)
The result is 9 (the maximum of [4,1,5,9])
sparseTableQuery cannot handle ranges of length 4; it returns -1
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: sparseTableQuery(st,2,5)=1; range [2..5]=[4,1,5,9]; min=1; k=floor(log2(4))=2; the two overlapping ranges: [2..5] (table[2][2]) and [2..5] (table[5-4+1][2]=table[2][2]); both return 1; min(1,1)=1 ✓.

logic_mcq.question: Module 2 has 2 NC150 problems (#307 and #315). Problem #315 'Count of Smaller Numbers After Self' uses 'Fenwick + coordinate compression'. What does coordinate compression enable here?
options: Coordinate compression sorts the array to enable binary search

COORDINATE COMPRESSION maps potentially large values (e.g., nums[i] up to 10^4) to SMALL INDICES (1..n) so the Fenwick tree's size is O(n) rather than O(max_value); for #315: to count smaller numbers to the right of each element, process right-to-left; compress values to rank 1..n; for each element at rank r, query(r-1) gives count of smaller already-seen elements; update(r, 1) registers the current element; without compression, the Fenwick tree would need size 10^4+1 even for n=5 elements
Coordinate compression converts the 2D problem to 1D
Compression is needed only when elements are negative
logic_mcq.explanation: Coordinate compression for Fenwick trees: map actual values to ranks 1..n; this bounds the Fenwick tree size to O(n) regardless of value magnitude; for #315, process right-to-left with a Fenwick tree tracking seen values by rank; query(rank-1) = count of elements already seen with rank < current rank = elements to the RIGHT (already processed) that are SMALLER; this gives O(n log n) solution vs O(n²) naive.

syntax_mcq.question: In `sparseTableQuery`, `const k = Math.floor(Math.log2(r - l + 1))` computes k once for O(1) query. Why is precomputing log values (not computing at query time) important for production?
options: Math.log2 is not available in all JavaScript environments

Math.log2 is a FLOATING-POINT OPERATION costing multiple CPU cycles; for O(1) queries to be practically fast, the log computation must not be the bottleneck; in production sparse tables with millions of queries, precomputing a LOG TABLE (log2[i] for i=1..n) converts the log lookup to O(1) array access (faster than computing Math.log2 each time); the lesson's implementation computes Math.log2 per query for simplicity; a production implementation would precompute: `const logTable = Array.from({length:n+1}, (_,i)=>Math.floor(Math.log2(i||1)))`
Math.log2 returns floating-point; the integer conversion via Math.floor is O(n)
Precomputing log values enables parallel processing of multiple queries
syntax_mcq.explanation: Production sparse table optimisation: precompute `log[i] = floor(log2(i))` for i=1..n as an O(n) array; query lookup then costs O(1) integer array access instead of O(1) floating-point log computation; for 10^8 queries, the constant factor matters; the lesson's Math.log2 approach is pedagogically clear and functionally O(1), but production code precomputes the log table.
